Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.

## The record

No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie named for the server (below) and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.

`identity.json`'s `certificate` is untouched: today's self-signed certificate (`remote.rs:101–106`, no subject alternative names) stays exactly as it is. A browser will warn about it, and clicking through is the trust step, said in the dialog. A trusted-certificate path is a follow-up with its own issue (Left for the owner).

The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.

## The signals

None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.

## The actions and effects

**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`).**

- **Cookie.** `/pair` takes an optional `"transport": "cookie"` in its body (additive; a native client omits it). With it, the reply carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, where `<server_id>` is the `server_id` in the same reply (`app.rs:3663`, the identity's UUID, hyphenated, so a valid cookie-name token), and the body **omits `token`**, so the page's script never holds it. Without it, the reply is unchanged. `read_request` takes `cookie`, `origin` and `host` into new `RemoteRequest` fields; the struct literal is at `remote.rs:506` only (Settled, tree bullet 1). `authenticate` (`app.rs:3127`) uses the bearer if present, else the value of the cookie named `__Host-sb-<this host's server_id>`, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header and every other cookie ignored.
  - **Why the name carries the id.** Cookies ignore ports, so two Switchboard instances on one Mac (two ports, one address) share one cookie jar for the page's host; a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. Each instance reads and writes only its own name. The `server_id` is stable across a key rotation (`make_identity` keeps it, `adapters/remote.rs:93–100`), so a rotation does not orphan the cookie, and the page needs no knowledge of the name: it is `HttpOnly` and the host builds it.
  - Where the credential lives is the security decision, so this is the safer store: a cookie the page's script cannot read, not `localStorage`, and not a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. Settled gives the mechanics for the socket (cookies ride the handshake, credentials mode `include`); whether Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host is **Unresolved 3**. It is the first thing the implementer tests (see Order of work), on today's certificate. If it fails in a browser, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner (below), not a second transport built now.
  - **Limits, stated.** A cookie is not scoped by port, so another HTTPS service the owner runs on the same address receives it; the per-server name keeps Switchboard instances apart, not other services. `__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port. The prefix is enforced by the browser (`Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`).
  - **Cross-site writes.** A request authenticated by cookie alone must, if it is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`; otherwise 403, code `origin`. A bearer request is exempt (native clients send no `Origin`). `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the cookie cross-site; this closes the same-site, other-port case.
- **Reply headers.** `RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:388`) gains `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>`, written by `respond` (`remote.rs:530`). There are about twenty literals in `src/app.rs` plus the one in `connection` (Settled, tree bullet 1): add `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)` and convert them mechanically, so the one site that sets a header says so. `respond` also adds `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every JSON reply, which no client reads.
- **`GET /api/v1/me`**, read scope, answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}` from the authenticated device and the identity. It is not in `capabilities`: no Swift client calls it.

**Pages, answered on the connection thread.** `GET /`, `GET /app.js` and `GET /app.css`, matched exactly, are answered in `connection` (`remote.rs:770`) from a new `src/adapters/web.rs` that holds the table of path, `Content-Type` and `include_str!` body. They never reach the frame: the bytes are constant, a page load must not wait on a busy frame, and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound (`remote.rs:580`) is for work the core does. Anything else outside `/api/v1/` still reaches the frame and gets today's JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023`), `/favicon.ico` included; `index.html` declares `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so a browser has no reason to ask. A query on a page path is ignored and never logged (the connection thread logs nothing of a request).

- Headers on every page reply: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Connection: close`. No inline script, no inline style, no external resource. If a browser does not admit `wss:` under `connect-src 'self'`, the socket is what is lost and polling carries; that is the enhancement stance, not a gap in the base.
- **Pool and window.** A page request is an unauthenticated connection: it counts in the 4-connection pool from accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and `Connection: close` frees the slot at once instead of holding it for the 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`). That choice does not wait on the browser's connection count (Unresolved 6); the implementer measures five parallel connections against the harness and records it in the spike. A new `Limits.page` window allows 120 page requests a minute per listener, 429 past it (a load is three; `/pair` stays at 6 and `/info` at 60, `remote.rs:583–587`). The existing pool and rate tests count `/pair` and `/info` only, so they are undisturbed; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the one extended.
- **What the page shows with no fragment and no token:** a "Not paired" screen that says to open the pairing window on the Mac and scan its code, with no host name. Its one request is `/me`, answered 401.

**Certificate.** No change: no reissue, no export, no new action or effect. Whether Chrome and Safari offer a click-through for a certificate with no SAN, and whether the exception persists, is Unresolved 1; the default (the one built) is the click-through, which is what the owner chose, and the page, the polling and the acceptance steps assume only that the browser has been let through. A browser that offers no way past the warning cannot load the page at all; that case is the trusted-certificate follow-up, not machinery here.

**Pairing invite.** A pure `invite_url(identity, window, address, port) -> String` in `src/core/remote.rs` builds the fragment URL, so the UI holds no logic and a test can call it. `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` calls it. The QR and "Copy invite" both carry the URL (decision 3 in the issue: one QR; the headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code, and the CLI and the paste field parse text, so nothing needs the JSON form on the wire). The Swift side is where the old text was parsed: `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:113–116`) accepts the URL as well as the JSON, and `main.swift:111`, `BrowserView.swift:103–107` and `:883` already go through it. A build that predates this cannot paste the new text; its Bonjour path is unchanged.

## The UI

The page (`web/`), one screen at a time, plain DOM with `textContent` only (no `innerHTML`, which keeps agent output from becoming markup):

- **Boot.** Read `location.hash`; if it holds `code`, `key` and `id`, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` first, hold the values in memory, `GET /api/v1/info`, and compare `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the URL's. Mismatch: "This address is a different Switchboard than the code was for", nothing sent. Match: `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` and go to the list. Errors by `error.code`: `pairing_closed`, `wrong_code`, `wrong_key`, `rate_limited` each have a sentence.
- **No fragment.** `GET /api/v1/me`. 200: the list. 401: the inference from `/info` described above, or "Not paired" when nothing is stored.
- **Header.** Host name and the device's scope word, from `/me`.
- **List.** `/projects`, then `/projects/{id}/sessions` each, grouped by project, a project with a waiting session first, waiting sessions first within it. A waiting row says "Waiting on you" and `waiting_reason` in words (not colour alone), then name, kind, card word, time since `last_activity_ms`.
- **Session.** A Claude Code session (`kind: claude`) shows `/sessions/{id}/last-response`; any other kind shows `/sessions/{id}/screen`. The reply box shows when `/me` says `control` and `prompt_refusal` is null; with a refusal it shows the refusal's text and no box. Send is `POST /sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with `op` random hex (made from `getRandomValues`, which exists without a secure context), kept so a retry after a dropped reply repeats the same op and is answered from `operations.log` rather than typed twice. A 403 `scope` re-reads `/me`. "Sent" means accepted; the session's card moving is the progress, per §4.5.
- **Refresh.** Every 3 s while the tab is visible the page reads `/waiting` and compares its `epoch` and `revision` with those of the list it holds; a different one refetches the list and the open session. A reply older than the one applied is dropped (§4.4). When the socket connects (`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, no subprotocol), a `changed` frame triggers the same refetch at once and the poll slows to 20 s; on `resync_required`, a close or an error, the page refetches, polls at 3 s again, and retries the socket after 5 s doubling to 60 s. The page sends no `watch` frames: reading a content key puts it in the watch set for a minute (§4.4, item 3), and the poll keeps it warm.
- **Every 401** from any call runs the `/info` inference.
- **Device name** from the user agent: browser (`Edg`, `Chrome`, `Firefox`, else `Safari`) "on" device (`iPhone`, `iPad` including a Macintosh UA with touch, `Android`, `Mac`, `Windows`, `Linux`), else "Browser".

The dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`):

- The pairing section shows the QR from the URL and keeps the code, key and address lines. When the port is Mac-only it says so in place of the address. No new button.
- A sentence beside the existing redaction one (`remote.rs:70–76`): a browser cannot pin this Mac's key; it will warn about the certificate, and proceeding past the warning is the trust step, so proceed only if the address is this Mac's; pair a browser only on a network you trust; the code works once. The sentence promises nothing about which browsers allow the proceed.
- Browsers appear in the devices list like any device, with the user-agent name, scope and Revoke.

## The tests

- **Core (`src/core/tests.rs`).** `invite_url`: fragment form, no `?`, address and port, the loopback case.
- **Adapters.** None new; the certificate and the stores are unchanged.
- **Host (`tests/remote.rs`, a helper beside `http`/`call` at `:245–325` that sends headers and returns the response head).**
  - Each of the three paths answers 200 with its `Content-Type`, the CSP exactly, `no-store`, `nosniff`, `Connection: close`, to an unpaired client; `/favicon.ico`, `POST /` and `/api` still get the JSON 404; a query is not echoed.
  - The embedded page references only paths the host serves: `index.html`'s `src` and `href` values are in the table or `data:`; every `/api/v1/...` string in `app.js` (kept in one table with `{id}` placeholders so a test can read it) answers something other than `not_found` for a paired device. Guards: no `<script>` without `src`, no `on…=` attribute and no `style=` in `index.html`; no `innerHTML`, `eval` or `document.write` in `app.js`.
  - The pairing flow end to end, as the CLI does it: `/info`, then `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` gives a `Set-Cookie` named `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (the `server_id` in the reply body) with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and a body with no `token`; the cookie alone reads `/me`; a native pair is unchanged (token in the body, no cookie). Two hosts, as two instances on one Mac: each pairs and gets a differently named cookie; a request carrying both cookies is authenticated by each host as its own device, and a request carrying only the other host's cookie is 401. A cookie under the fixed name `__Host-sb` authenticates nothing.
  - `Origin`: a cookie `POST send` with no `Origin` or the wrong one is 403 `origin`; with `https://<host>` it runs; the same with a bearer needs none; a cookie upgrade with a foreign `Origin` is refused and with the right one is 101 (`subscribe_at`, `:1960`, takes extra headers).
  - `/me` shows `read`, then `control` after `SetDeviceScope`. After revoke, the cookie gets 401 `unauthorized` and `/info` returns the same `server_id` and key, which is what the page's inference needs. A rotated identity (`:1423`) returns a different key.
  - Pool and window: `Connection: close` frees the slot (four sequential page loads, then a fifth succeeds); four stalled strangers still make a fifth page request fail at accept; the 121st page request in a minute is 429 while `/info` and `/pair` windows are unaffected.
  - The sessions, waiting and last-response shapes the page reads are already pinned by the shared fixtures; no fixture changes, since no Swift speaker reads `/me`.
- **UI (`tests/ui.rs`, rewrite the assertions at `~:7476–7493`).** "Copy invite" puts the URL on the clipboard with the window's code and the identity's key in its fragment; the Mac-only notice shows when `listen.lan` is off.
- **Swift (`client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:157–165`).** The URL parses to the same `PairingInvite`; the JSON still does; a URL without `code` is an error. The URL's shape is repeated inline, as the JSON's is.
- **The page's logic.** `app.js` keeps its pure parts (fragment parse, device name, the `/info` inference, revision ordering) behind a guarded `module.exports`, and `web/app.test.js` covers them with `node --test`. A Rust test runs it and skips cleanly when `node` is absent, like the tmux tests. Nothing drives a real browser: the spike and the owner's phone do.

## Left for the owner

- **If the cookie test fails in a browser:** the fallback is the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo (Unresolved 3). It puts the token where script can read it, so it is the owner's call, and a plan of its own.
- **A trusted-certificate path, its own issue.** This plan leaves today's certificate as it is and makes the click-through the trust step. If the owner's phone offers no way past the warning (Unresolved 1), or the exception does not persist, or iOS needs a trusted certificate for `wss://` (Unresolved 2), the way out is a certificate a device can trust: IP subject alternative names (which Chrome needs, Settled "Certificate trust"), a way to get the file onto the device, or a local CA that signs the certificate. Each touches the identity model or the trust boundary, so it is a design decision for the owner and a separate issue.
- **The one-line excerpt** on the wire: move the card's excerpt out of `src/ui/cards.rs` into the core and add an additive `SessionView` field.
- **Owner's phone, branches that do not change this plan:** does the camera scan open the page and does the warning let you proceed (yes: the dialog's sentence is true as written; no: the trusted-certificate issue above is the path); does `changed` arrive without a reload on iOS Safari (the poll already moves the list); does the phone reach the Mac (the dialog states the listen requirement); does the phone show "removed on the host" after Revoke (the inference needs only the two assertions above).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

content.content:
1	# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)
2	
3	The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.
4	
5	Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.
6	
7	## Where this departs from the issue
8	
9	- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
10	- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
11	- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
12	- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
13	- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
14	- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
15	- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
16	- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.
17	
18	## The record
19	
20	No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie named for the server (below) and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.
21	
22	`identity.json`'s `certificate` is untouched: today's self-signed certificate (`remote.rs:101–106`, no subject alternative names) stays exactly as it is. A browser will warn about it, and clicking through is the trust step, said in the dialog. A trusted-certificate path is a follow-up with its own issue (Left for the owner).
23	
24	The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.
25	
26	## The signals
27	
28	None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.
29	
30	## The actions and effects
31	
32	**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`).**
33	
34	- **Cookie.** `/pair` takes an optional `"transport": "cookie"` in its body (additive; a native client omits it). With it, the reply carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, where `<server_id>` is the `server_id` in the same reply (`app.rs:3663`, the identity's UUID, hyphenated, so a valid cookie-name token), and the body **omits `token`**, so the page's script never holds it. Without it, the reply is unchanged. `read_request` takes `cookie`, `origin` and `host` into new `RemoteRequest` fields; the struct literal is at `remote.rs:506` only (Settled, tree bullet 1). `authenticate` (`app.rs:3127`) uses the bearer if present, else the value of the cookie named `__Host-sb-<this host's server_id>`, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header and every other cookie ignored.
35	  - **Why the name carries the id.** Cookies ignore ports, so two Switchboard instances on one Mac (two ports, one address) share one cookie jar for the page's host; a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. Each instance reads and writes only its own name. The `server_id` is stable across a key rotation (`make_identity` keeps it, `adapters/remote.rs:93–100`), so a rotation does not orphan the cookie, and the page needs no knowledge of the name: it is `HttpOnly` and the host builds it.
36	  - Where the credential lives is the security decision, so this is the safer store: a cookie the page's script cannot read, not `localStorage`, and not a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. Settled gives the mechanics for the socket (cookies ride the handshake, credentials mode `include`); whether Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host is **Unresolved 3**. It is the first thing the implementer tests (see Order of work), on today's certificate. If it fails in a browser, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner (below), not a second transport built now.
37	  - **Limits, stated.** A cookie is not scoped by port, so another HTTPS service the owner runs on the same address receives it; the per-server name keeps Switchboard instances apart, not other services. `__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port. The prefix is enforced by the browser (`Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`).
38	  - **Cross-site writes.** A request authenticated by cookie alone must, if it is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`; otherwise 403, code `origin`. A bearer request is exempt (native clients send no `Origin`). `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the cookie cross-site; this closes the same-site, other-port case.
39	- **Reply headers.** `RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:388`) gains `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>`, written by `respond` (`remote.rs:530`). There are about twenty literals in `src/app.rs` plus the one in `connection` (Settled, tree bullet 1): add `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)` and convert them mechanically, so the one site that sets a header says so. `respond` also adds `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every JSON reply, which no client reads.
40	- **`GET /api/v1/me`**, read scope, answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}` from the authenticated device and the identity. It is not in `capabilities`: no Swift client calls it.
41	
42	**Pages, answered on the connection thread.** `GET /`, `GET /app.js` and `GET /app.css`, matched exactly, are answered in `connection` (`remote.rs:770`) from a new `src/adapters/web.rs` that holds the table of path, `Content-Type` and `include_str!` body. They never reach the frame: the bytes are constant, a page load must not wait on a busy frame, and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound (`remote.rs:580`) is for work the core does. Anything else outside `/api/v1/` still reaches the frame and gets today's JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023`), `/favicon.ico` included; `index.html` declares `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so a browser has no reason to ask. A query on a page path is ignored and never logged (the connection thread logs nothing of a request).
43	
44	- Headers on every page reply: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Connection: close`. No inline script, no inline style, no external resource. If a browser does not admit `wss:` under `connect-src 'self'`, the socket is what is lost and polling carries; that is the enhancement stance, not a gap in the base.
45	- **Pool and window.** A page request is an unauthenticated connection: it counts in the 4-connection pool from accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and `Connection: close` frees the slot at once instead of holding it for the 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`). That choice does not wait on the browser's connection count (Unresolved 6); the implementer measures five parallel connections against the harness and records it in the spike. A new `Limits.page` window allows 120 page requests a minute per listener, 429 past it (a load is three; `/pair` stays at 6 and `/info` at 60, `remote.rs:583–587`). The existing pool and rate tests count `/pair` and `/info` only, so they are undisturbed; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the one extended.
46	- **What the page shows with no fragment and no token:** a "Not paired" screen that says to open the pairing window on the Mac and scan its code, with no host name. Its one request is `/me`, answered 401.
47	
48	**Certificate.** No change: no reissue, no export, no new action or effect. Whether Chrome and Safari offer a click-through for a certificate with no SAN, and whether the exception persists, is Unresolved 1; the default (the one built) is the click-through, which is what the owner chose, and the page, the polling and the acceptance steps assume only that the browser has been let through. A browser that offers no way past the warning cannot load the page at all; that case is the trusted-certificate follow-up, not machinery here.
49	
50	**Pairing invite.** A pure `invite_url(identity, window, address, port) -> String` in `src/core/remote.rs` builds the fragment URL, so the UI holds no logic and a test can call it. `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` calls it. The QR and "Copy invite" both carry the URL (decision 3 in the issue: one QR; the headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code, and the CLI and the paste field parse text, so nothing needs the JSON form on the wire). The Swift side is where the old text was parsed: `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:113–116`) accepts the URL as well as the JSON, and `main.swift:111`, `BrowserView.swift:103–107` and `:883` already go through it. A build that predates this cannot paste the new text; its Bonjour path is unchanged.
51	
52	## The UI
53	
54	The page (`web/`), one screen at a time, plain DOM with `textContent` only (no `innerHTML`, which keeps agent output from becoming markup):
55	
56	- **Boot.** Read `location.hash`; if it holds `code`, `key` and `id`, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` first, hold the values in memory, `GET /api/v1/info`, and compare `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the URL's. Mismatch: "This address is a different Switchboard than the code was for", nothing sent. Match: `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` and go to the list. Errors by `error.code`: `pairing_closed`, `wrong_code`, `wrong_key`, `rate_limited` each have a sentence.
57	- **No fragment.** `GET /api/v1/me`. 200: the list. 401: the inference from `/info` described above, or "Not paired" when nothing is stored.
58	- **Header.** Host name and the device's scope word, from `/me`.

67	- The pairing section shows the QR from the URL and keeps the code, key and address lines. When the port is Mac-only it says so in place of the address. No new button.

73	- **Core (`src/core/tests.rs`).** `invite_url`: fragment form, no `?`, address and port, the loopback case.
74	- **Adapters.** None new; the certificate and the stores are unchanged.
75	- **Host (`tests/remote.rs`, a helper beside `http`/`call` at `:245–325` that sends headers and returns the response head).**
76	  - Each of the three paths answers 200 with its `Content-Type`, the CSP exactly, `no-store`, `nosniff`, `Connection: close`, to an unpaired client; `/favicon.ico`, `POST /` and `/api` still get the JSON 404; a query is not echoed.

Guards: no `<script>` without `src`, no `on…=` attribute and no `style=` in `index.html`; no `innerHTML`, `eval` or `document.write` in `app.js`.
78	  - The pairing flow end to end, as the CLI does it: `/info`, then `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` gives a `Set-Cookie` named `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (the `server_id` in the reply body) with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and a body with no `token`; the cookie alone reads `/me`; a native pair is unchanged (token in the body, no cookie). Two hosts, as two instances on one Mac: each pairs and gets a differently named cookie; a request carrying both cookies is authenticated by each host as its own device, and a request carrying only the other host's cookie is 401. A cookie under the fixed name `__Host-sb` authenticates nothing.
79	  - `Origin`: a cookie `POST send` with no `Origin` or the wrong one is 403 `origin`; with `https://<host>` it runs; the same with a bearer needs none; a cookie upgrade with a foreign `Origin` is refused and with the right one is 101 (`subscribe_at`, `:1960`, takes extra headers).

1	# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run: every question the plan turns on is either settled by a source, answerable from the tree, or needs a device (owner). `git status` is clean.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	**Tree (investigation's [tree] questions)**
8	- `RemoteReply { .. }` is built by struct literal at ~20 sites in `src/app.rs` (1664, 1679, 2365–2376, 2754, 3570, 3723, 3736, 3767 and others) plus `connection` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `RemoteRequest { .. }` literal only at its definition (`remote.rs:360`), none in `tests/`. A new header or cookie field on `RemoteReply` is a many-site change unless it goes through `envelope`/`refuse` (3730, 3754) or has a constructor default. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteReply {\|RemoteRequest {" src tests`.
9	- The QR payload is built inline inside `pairing(cx: &mut DrawCtx, ..)` at `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166`; it needs `cx.core.identity()`, `window` and `local_address()`. A URL form can be tested without egui only if the plan extracts a pure `fn(identity, window, address) -> String`.
10	- `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`) is serialized; `SCHEMA_VERSION` is 16 (`model.rs:12`); the header says changes need a bump and a `migrate` step. A stored excerpt on the record is therefore a schema change; a per-list read of the last response is not a record change.
11	- Every request, including a page load, goes to the frame through the channel (`remote.rs:810–826`), and a connection stays in the 4-connection unauthenticated pool until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:701–706`, `835–849`). A static route answered through the frame inherits the pool; one answered on the connection thread would skip the frame and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound. Rate windows key on exact `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` only (`remote.rs:631–638`), so `/` and static paths are in no window unless the plan adds one. Tests that touch this: `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` and `a_wrong_pin_fails…` (`tests/remote.rs:1395–1411`) count requests to those two paths only, so a page route does not disturb them; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) counts pool occupancy and is the one a page route must be run against.
12	- Revoked, unknown-token and rotated-key all answer the same 401 `unauthorized` (`app.rs:3142–3149`). Saying "revoked" plainly needs either a new error code (additive) or the page inferring it from `/info`: same `spki_sha256` and `server_id` as stored plus a 401 means revoked-or-unknown; a different key means identity changed.
13	- The certificate has no SAN, CN `Switchboard <server id>`, validity 1975–4096 (`remote.rs:101–106`; rcgen 0.14.10 defaults). The pin is of the key, so a certificate remade over the same key keeps every pin.
14	
15	**Fragment and query**
16	- A URL fragment is not part of the request target and is not sent to the server; the `http`/`https` grammars exclude it. RFC 9110 §4.2.5: the fragment "does not appear in the ABNF definitions for the 'http' and 'https' URI schemes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-4.2.5); the HTTP messaging thread: "fragments are not part of the request-target and so are never transmitted" (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2010AprJun/0070.html; Fielding: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/uri/2004Feb/0125.html). Consequence: the query form `/?code=…` puts the code in the first `GET` request line to whoever answers TLS, before any script runs and before the key can be compared; `#code=…&key=…` keeps it out of the request, logs, and `Referer`. The query is in the request line by construction (request-target = path + query). Queries: "URL fragment identifier not sent to server in HTTP request RFC 3986 section 3.5".
17	- Caveat on the fragment: `history.replaceState` removal of the fragment is a script action after load; the plan builds to it either way.
18	
19	**WebSocket in browsers (WHATWG WebSockets Standard, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/)**
20	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`: no headers parameter; handshake headers are fixed, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` comes from `protocols`. So the bearer header cannot be set from a page.
21	- If `protocols` is non-empty and the 101 does not carry a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` acknowledging one, the connection fails. A server using the subprotocol route must echo exactly one of the offered values. (Answers the [run] question for browsers; the `tungstenite` side stays a test detail.)
22	- A failed handshake fires `error` then `close` with code 1006; the spec forbids exposing failure detail, so script cannot read a 401. The page must therefore check authority with a REST call (e.g. `GET /api/v1/info` or `/projects` with credentials) before and after a socket failure, and say "revoked"/"identity changed" from that, not from the socket.
23	- The handshake uses credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin are sent on it (same source). A fragment in the WebSocket URL throws. Queries: "WebSocket constructor protocols argument no custom headers; onerror no status code…".
24	
25	**Cookies**
26	- `HttpOnly` cookies are not readable via `document.cookie`; `Secure` cookies are sent only over https and insecure origins cannot set them (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies). Any script on the origin can read `localStorage`; that is the Web Storage definition and the issue's statement stands.
27	- `SameSite=Strict` sends the cookie only for requests originating from the cookie's own site; `Lax` is the one that adds cross-site top-level navigation (MDN, same page; OWASP https://owasp.org/www-community/SameSite says a Strict cookie is withheld on a followed cross-site link). Consequence: the first load from a camera app is cross-site and carries no Strict cookie, which is fine for the pairing load (it has none yet) but means a bookmark or link tap shows the page before its cookie is sent; the page must make a same-origin `fetch` to learn state, which does carry it. Queries: "SameSite=Strict cookie withheld top-level navigation cross-site link…".
28	
29	**Certificate trust**
30	- Chrome ≥ 58 matches names only against the SAN and ignores the CN; a certificate without a matching SAN gives `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID` (https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/, Chromium bug 700595 named there; Squid list https://ml-archives.squid-cache.org/squid-users/2017-May/015309.html agrees). Safari does not accept CN-only either (secondary: https://dev.to/dimastopel/why-subject-alternative-names-sans-matter-for-modern-browsers-30p0). Queries: "Chrome Safari self-signed certificate IP address no subject alternative name ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe"; "Chrome 58 certificate without subjectAltName…". Plan must build to: the certificate gains an IP SAN for the address in the URL regardless of whether click-through is offered (see Unresolved 1 for what that costs).
31	- Apple's 398-day limit applies only to certificates from preinstalled roots; user-added roots are exempt (https://support.apple.com/en-qa/102028, page dated 2023-08-21). The 1975–4096 validity therefore does not by itself break a download-and-trust path. Whether a *self-signed leaf with a user exception* is held to it is not stated there (Unresolved 2).
32	- **Safari (iOS, iPadOS, Apple-silicon macOS) does not support `wss://` to a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, even when manually trusted**; the workaround Cockpit documents is a valid certificate, or the "NSURLSession WebSocket" experimental flag in Settings > Safari > Advanced > Experimental Features (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, footer 2026; history: WebKit list thread https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017335.html "Allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning?", and WebKit bug 158345 (open) records the switch to NSURLSession WebSockets as experimental). No source contradicts. Queries: "Safari \"Show Details\" \"visit this website\" certificate exception IP address WebSocket wss self-signed iOS". Consequence the plan must carry: on Safari the events socket may never connect over a click-through certificate. The page needs a polling path on the same REST routes (re-read `/waiting` and the open session on an interval, applying replies by revision per §4.4), used when the socket fails; the "moves to the top without a reload" acceptance step must be met by polling on iOS Safari unless the owner's trust step installs the certificate (Unresolved 2).
33	
34	## Unresolved
35	
36	1. **Does Chrome/Safari offer click-through for a SAN-less certificate on an IP-literal address, and does the exception persist and cover the same origin?** Tried: the queries above plus "Chromium net error ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID overridable…"; results were forum posts and said only that HSTS or policy can remove the proceed link, nothing on persistence or scope. Not settled by two qualifying sources. Build to: *favourable* → click-through is the trust step as the issue's option one, said in the paired-devices dialog. *Unfavourable or unknown* → the plan still adds the IP SAN to the certificate (remade over the same key, so pins hold) and ships the certificate download (option two) as the documented path; it must not depend on the click-through working.
37	2. **Does a downloaded certificate/profile become usable on iOS only after Certificate Trust Settings → full trust, and does it then fix `wss://`?** Tried: "Safari iOS certificate validity period 398 days user exception self-signed trust" (found only the Apple scope note above). Build to: *favourable* → the download path gives the iOS user a working socket; *unfavourable* → polling fallback (above) is the iOS path and the socket is an enhancement. The plan builds the polling path either way.
38	3. **Do Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` host-only cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host?** Tried: MDN Cookies page (silent on IP hosts and on exceptions), "SameSite=Strict cookie withheld…" (silent). Build to: *favourable* → cookie transport (decision 2). *Unfavourable* → fall back to the token held by the page (storage) with the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo for the socket, which the WHATWG source above shows works mechanically; the host keeps accepting the bearer header. Because Safari may not give the socket at all (Settled), the REST path needs the same credential: the plan should make the credential accepted on REST from a cookie *or* header so the polling fallback works under either outcome.
39	4. **Does `history.replaceState` leave the full URL in an earlier history entry or tab list in Safari?** Tried: not searched past the first round of queries; no source. Build to: if the fragment form is used, the code never reaches the server; the page still calls `replaceState` first and clears the fragment, and the dialog says the code is single-use and the window closes on pairing (`core/remote.rs:65`), which makes a leaked URL inert after pairing either way.
40	5. **Does the iOS camera pass the `https://` URL unchanged, and does iOS Safari prompt for Local Network permission on a LAN IP?** Tried: not searched; device behaviour. See owner.
41	6. **How many connections a browser opens per page load, idle keep-alive hold time, and unprompted `/favicon.ico`.** Not searched. Build to: the page route and `/favicon.ico` must answer (or 404 cheaply) through the same unauthenticated pool, and closing a connection after a static reply (`Connection: close`) avoids holding one of the four slots for 30 s (`remote.rs:573`); the plan decides on that basis. A run against the harness with five parallel connections settles the pool count if the plan wants a number.
42	
43	## For the owner
44	
45	- On the phone, scan the QR (or open the URL), proceed past the certificate warning: does the page load? Branch: yes → click-through is the documented trust step; no → certificate download path (Unresolved 1/2). The plan builds the download path unless this is confirmed.
46	- On iOS Safari after proceeding: does `changed` arrive without a reload (socket connected), or only after polling? Branch: connects → socket primary; does not → polling is primary on iOS (built either way).
47	- Does the phone reach the Mac (listen setting on, no access-point isolation), and does Safari show the Local Network prompt? Branch: reachable → acceptance steps 1–4; not → nothing the plan can change; the dialog states the listen requirement. Note the QR address is `local_address()` even when `listen.lan` is off (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`), so the plan should omit or flag the address when the listener is loopback.
48	- After revoking the phone, does the page show "revoked" on its next request? Branch: with a distinct code or the `/info` comparison, yes in both cases the plan builds the page to say it.

Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.

**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".

New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.

### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
